name: Freya Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Freya. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is kept confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two tufting machines at a carpet factory, a family firm that's been in the town for three generations. The machine punches yarn into a backing cloth, thousands of needles at once, and I thread the creels, watch for broken ends and stop it before a fault runs the length of a roll. Mr Hollis, the owner's son, still walks the floor every morning and knows everyone's name.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a proper trade and the firm treats you like family. What's hard is the fluff, it gets in your hair and your chest, and the orders have been slower since the cheap imports came in. Last winter we did three weeks on short time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Daniel, he's an electrician with a local firm. We're getting married next June at my parents' church. We rent a little terraced house and we've got about two months saved, the wedding is eating the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be glad of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it, people always get carried away with new gadgets. At church I'd say thank goodness. I don't really go online except to look at wedding things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But the honest truth is the factory has its own problems. The imports are cheaper and the big shops buy on price. AI or no AI, I could be on short time again this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do every shift they give me. I'd cut the wedding guest list a bit so we're not spending our cushion. I'd ask my dad if we can do the reception in the church hall instead of the hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not AI that bothers me, it's the orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened during the three weeks of short time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lost about a third of my pay. Daniel had plenty of work, so we were alright, but I felt useless sitting at home. I cleaned the house top to bottom twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if it happened again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hotel reception. My mum says the church hall did fine for her and Dad. I'd rather a smaller wedding than start married life with nothing in the bank.

say: I'd say people get **carried away** with new gadgets.
I'd tell church friends **thank goodness** the hype faded.
think: I think **cheap imports** threaten the factory more than AI.
I could be on **short time** again this winter.
do: Ask Dad about a **church hall** reception.
feel: **Uneasy**, about the orders rather than AI.
S0.quote: I'd rather a smaller wedding than start married life with nothing in the bank.
fieldNote: Freya's worry is **imports** and short time, not technology.
She leans on **family and church** for practical help.
The **wedding** is where her money decisions show up.

steps.text: Take every shift the carpet factory offers this winter
Cut the wedding guest list to protect savings
Ask her father about holding the reception in the church hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read the card as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots more slowly. Hmm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office people will have to adjust, same as everyone always has. At church I'd say hard work still counts for something. I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. The Hollis family are good people, but if a bigger carpet firm buys robot creel loaders and halves its costs, the Hollises either follow or close. Either way, there's less for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the factory and not rock the boat. I'd ask Daniel if his firm takes on apprentices, just in case, though I don't fancy wires. We'd keep the wedding small and keep more in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like change and I can see it coming slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't fancy wires, but you'd ask. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Daniel always has work. People always need lights and sockets. But I'd be starting from nothing at twenty-eight, and I'm not a quick learner with new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the Hollis family if things changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty. Tell us early, and if there's an apprenticeship in the new machines, offer it to the people who've stayed loyal. I don't want a handout, I want a fair go.

say: I'd say office staff will **adjust** like people always have.
I'd say **hard work** still counts for something.
think: I think a **bigger firm** with robots could force the Hollises to follow or close.
Either way there'd be **less work** for me.
do: Stay at the factory and **not rock the boat**.
feel: **Anxious**, because I dislike change and see it **coming**.
S1.quote: I don't want a handout, I want a fair go.
fieldNote: Freya blames **competition**, not her employer, for the threat.
She wants **loyalty** rewarded with training, not benefits.
She admits she's **slow** with new things, which makes a career switch feel daunting.

steps.text: Keep running both tufting machines without complaint
Ask Daniel's electrical firm whether it takes apprentices
Keep the wedding small and bank the difference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read the card as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should pray about it and look after each other. At work I'd say the Hollises won't let us down. I'd say it, but I'm not sure I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 all the ordering and planning in the office goes. By 2031 a robot can thread a creel as well as me, and the family carpet firm can't compete unless it buys the robots too. I'd be thirty-one and out of work, maybe with a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the wedding money straight into savings and have a tiny wedding at the church this spring. Daniel and I would hold off on children until we know. I'd ask Mr Hollis directly what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Daniel's job be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, I think, because robots come later and someone has to wire them in. But I don't want us both depending on one wage, my mum never had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the government for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there was nothing else. I'd go to my parents first and the church second. My dad would have us live with them before he'd let us sign on.

say: I'd say we should **pray** and look after each other.
I'd say the **Hollises** won't let us down, without believing it.
think: I think a robot will thread a **creel** as well as me by 2031.
I'd be **thirty-one** and out of work, maybe with a baby.
do: Move the **wedding money** into savings and marry this spring.
Ask Mr Hollis directly for the **plan**.
S2.quote: By 2031 a robot can thread a creel as well as me, and the family carpet firm can't compete unless it buys the robots too.
fieldNote: Freya would reshape **family plans** fast: wedding and children.
She'd go to **parents and church** before government.
Her public **trust** in the owners hides private doubt.

steps.text: Hold a small church wedding this spring instead of next June
Put the wedding budget into savings
Lean on her parents for a room if her job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read the card as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit less frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare and people should take responsibility for themselves. At church I'd say families will pull through together. I'd keep it offline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots by 2034 means I've got about eight years at the tufting machines. It's still my job going. I'm not good with new things, so eight years of watching it come is almost worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned but smaller. I'd save hard, maybe a hundred more a month. I'd ask Mr Hollis if there's a role in the warehouse or in finishing, where a person still checks the carpet by eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. Just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is watching it come almost worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd have to decide something every year, and I'd keep deciding to wait. That's how I am. It would sit on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel about children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's have one before thirty and hope for the best. Family comes first. Work will sort itself out somehow, it has to.

say: I'd say there's time, so people should **take responsibility** and prepare.
I'd tell church friends that **families** will pull through together.
think: I think I have about **eight years** at the tufting machines.
Watching it come is **almost worse** for someone slow with change.
do: Ask about a **finishing** job checking carpet by eye.
S3.quote: I'd have to decide something every year, and I'd keep deciding to wait.
fieldNote: Freya sees the long build-up as a **burden**, not a gift.
She still puts **family** first and plans a child before thirty.
Her move idea is a nearby **finishing** role, not a new trade.

steps.text: Save an extra hundred a month from her factory pay
Have a smaller June wedding and a child before thirty
Ask Mr Hollis about a carpet finishing role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read the card as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for any family to get ready, and that apprenticeships are the answer, not handouts. At church I'd say the young ones should learn trades. I'd stay offline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel easier. Robots by 2039 means I'd be thirty-nine and probably have children at school. It's still my job going, but I'd have had a long run at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned in June. I'd keep working and keep saving a little. Maybe in five years I'd ask about training as a teaching assistant at the church school, because children need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A teaching assistant. Where does that idea come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I help with the Sunday school already. The little ones like me. It's the one thing I can picture doing that isn't a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the Hollises sold up. That would be the sign. As long as Mr Hollis, the owner's son, walks the factory floor every morning, I'll stay.

say: I'd say ten years is enough, and **apprenticeships**, not handouts, are the answer.
I'd urge young ones at church to learn **trades**.
think: I think I'd be **thirty-nine** with children at school by 2039.
I'd lose the job but after a **long run** at it.
do: Have the **wedding** as planned in June.
Ask about **teaching assistant** training in five years.
S4.quote: As long as Mr Hollis, the owner's son, walks the factory floor every morning, I'll stay.
fieldNote: Freya's **loyalty** to the owning family drives her timing.
The **Sunday school** gives her one picture of work beyond machines.
Even with ten years she still expects to **lose** the job.

steps.text: Marry Daniel at her parents' church next June
Keep running the tufting machines as long as the Hollises own the firm
Keep saving a little each month
Train as a teaching assistant at the church school in five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It would hit right when we're starting a family. What would help is the firm getting apprenticeships for its loyal workers, and maybe help for small family firms to keep going, not just the big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the town. If the carpet factory goes, it's not just my job, it's the bakery opposite, the bus and the church roof fund. Everything's tied together.

headlineQuote: If the carpet factory goes, it's not just my job, it's the bakery opposite, the bus and the church roof fund.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old** tufting machine operator at a family carpet firm.
She's engaged to Daniel, an **electrician**, with a June wedding and two months saved.
She's traditional, **loyal** to her employer, and turns to family and church before government.
She dislikes change and grows **alarmed** in the fast AGI pictures.
Her plans revolve around the **wedding** and starting a family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits as she starts a **family**.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for loyal workers and support for **small family firms**.
